claim: Infection of livestock by African trypanosomes has a significant effect on food production in sub-Saharan Africa.
source: Infection of livestock by African trypanosomes has a significant effect on food production in sub-Saharan Africa (Shaw et al., 2004).

claim: Human disease is caused by a restricted set of subspecies of Trypanosoma brucei.
source: In contrast to human disease, which is caused by a restricted set of subspecies of Trypanosoma brucei (Laveran, 1902; Pays and Vanhollebeke, 2009)

claim: Livestock disease is caused by at least six distinct species of African trypanosome, the most prevalent being T. congolense and T. vivax.

claim: T. brucei epimastigotes attach to the epithelium in the salivary glands away from the digestive tract.

claim: T. congolense and T. vivax epimastigotes attach in the proboscis within the digestive tract.

evidence: Supported by citations to Hoare, 1972; Peacock et al., 2012; Jefferies et al., 1987

claim: The cell surface of an African trypanosome acts as the molecular interface with its host.
source: The cell surface of an African trypanosome acts as the molecular interface with its host, and the developmental transitions of the life cycle involve radical changes in cell surface composition, presumably as adaptations to different host niches.
evidence: Based on established understanding of trypanosome biology

claim: The developmental transitions of the life cycle involve radical changes in cell surface composition, presumably as adaptations to different host niches.
source: The cell surface of an African trypanosome acts as the molecular interface with its host, and the developmental transitions of the life cycle involve radical changes in cell surface composition, presumably as adaptations to different host niches.
evidence: Speculative reasoning about the purpose of cell surface changes

claim: The cell surface of the mammalian bloodstream form is covered with a dense layer of variant surface glycoprotein (VSG).
source: The best understood stage is the mammalian bloodstream form where the cell surface is covered with a dense layer of variant surface glycoprotein (VSG), which acts to protect the plasma membrane, enhancing survival of individual cells and allowing antigenic variation to ensure population survival (Schwede and Carrington, 2010; Horn, 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to Schwede and Carrington, 2010; Horn, 2014

claim: VSG acts to protect the plasma membrane, enhancing survival of individual cells and allowing antigenic variation to ensure population survival.
source: The best understood stage is the mammalian bloodstream form where the cell surface is covered with a dense layer of variant surface glycoprotein (VSG), which acts to protect the plasma membrane, enhancing survival of individual cells and allowing antigenic variation to ensure population survival (Schwede and Carrington, 2010; Horn, 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to Schwede and Carrington, 2010; Horn, 2014

claim: The density of packing of the VSG molecules on the surface of the bloodstream form trypanosome is thought to approach the maximum possible.
source: The density of packing of the VSG molecules on the surface of the bloodstream form trypanosome is thought to approach the maximum possible (Grünfelder et al., 2002).
evidence: Supported by citation to Grünfelder et al., 2002

claim: The developmental stages found inside insects have less densely packed surface coats than bloodstream forms.
source: In contrast, the developmental stages found inside insects, including the procyclic and epimastigote forms, have less densely packed surface coats, and contain different sets of surface proteins, including GARP in T. congolense and procyclins and BARP in T. brucei (Bayne et al., 1993; Roditi et al., 1989; Urwyler et al., 2007; Beecroft et al., 1993).
evidence: Supported by citations to Bayne et al., 1993; Roditi et al., 1989; Urwyler et al., 2007; Beecroft et al., 1993

claim: Insect stage developmental forms contain different sets of surface proteins, including GARP in T. congolense and procyclins and BARP in T. brucei.
source: In contrast, the developmental stages found inside insects, including the procyclic and epimastigote forms, have less densely packed surface coats, and contain different sets of surface proteins, including GARP in T. congolense and procyclins and BARP in T. brucei (Bayne et al., 1993; Roditi et al., 1989; Urwyler et al., 2007; Beecroft et al., 1993).
evidence: Supported by citations to Bayne et al., 1993; Roditi et al., 1989; Urwyler et al., 2007; Beecroft et al., 1993

claim: TbHpHbR is expressed in the mammalian bloodstream form and is used for the uptake of haptoglobin-haemoglobin complexes for haem acquisition.
source: It is expressed in the mammalian bloodstream form and is used for the uptake of haptoglobin-haemoglobin complexes (HpHb) for haem acquisition (Vanhollebeke et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citation to Vanhollebeke et al., 2008

claim: Human serum contains two complexes, trypanolytic factors-1 and -2 (TLF1 and TLF2), which cause trypanosome lysis.
source: Human serum contains two complexes, trypanolytic factors-1 and -2 (TLF1 and TLF2), which cause trypanosome lysis (Rifkin, 1978; Hajduk et al., 1989; Tomlinson et al., 1995; Raper et al., 1996).
evidence: Supported by citations to Rifkin, 1978; Hajduk et al., 1989; Tomlinson et al., 1995; Raper et al., 1996

claim: TLF1 and TLF2 both contain the apolipoprotein L1 toxin.
source: TLF1 and TLF2 both contain the apolipoprotein L1 toxin (Vanhamme et al., 2003) and a complex of haemoglobin bound to haptoglobin-related protein (HprHb) (Raper et al., 1996).
evidence: Supported by citation to Vanhamme et al., 2003

claim: TLF1 and TLF2 both contain a complex of haemoglobin bound to haptoglobin-related protein (HprHb).
source: TLF1 and TLF2 both contain the apolipoprotein L1 toxin (Vanhamme et al., 2003) and a complex of haemoglobin bound to haptoglobin-related protein (HprHb) (Raper et al., 1996).
evidence: Supported by citation to Raper et al., 1996

claim: The binding of HprHb to TbHpHbR provides the uptake route for TLF1 into the trypanosome.
source: It is the binding of HprHb to TbHpHbR that provides the uptake route for TLF1 into the trypanosome (Vanhollebeke et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citation to Vanhollebeke et al., 2008

claim: The N-terminal domain of TbHpHbR is formed from an extended three α-helical bundle with a small, membrane-distal head.
source: The N-terminal domain of TbHpHbR is formed from an extended three α-helical bundle with a small, membrane-distal head, and is attached to the plasma membrane by a glycophosphatidylinosotol-anchor at the C-terminus of a small C-terminal domain.
evidence: Based on structural data from previous studies

claim: TbHpHbR is attached to the plasma membrane by a glycophosphatidylinosotol-anchor at the C-terminus of a small C-terminal domain.
source: The N-terminal domain of TbHpHbR is formed from an extended three α-helical bundle with a small, membrane-distal head, and is attached to the plasma membrane by a glycophosphatidylinosotol-anchor at the C-terminus of a small C-terminal domain.
evidence: Based on structural data from previous studies

claim: HpHb binds along the membrane-distal half of the helical bundle of TbHpHbR.
source: HpHb binds along the membrane-distal half of the helical bundle.
evidence: Based on structural data from previous studies

claim: The helical bundle of TbHpHbR has a ~50° kink between the HpHb binding site and the membrane attachment point.
source: A striking feature of this helical bundle is a ~50° kink, which lies between the HpHb binding site and the membrane attachment point.
evidence: Based on structural data from previous studies

claim: The kink in TbHpHbR is likely to result in separation of the VSG molecules on either side of the receptor, holding them apart and presenting the HpHb binding site to the extracellular environment.
source: This kink is likely to result in separation of the VSG molecules on either side of the receptor, holding them apart and presenting the HpHb binding site to the extracellular environment.
evidence: Inference based on structural features

claim: The kink in TbHpHbR allows two receptors to contact a single HpHb dimer, allowing greater avidity for the ligand and more efficient uptake into trypanosomes.
source: It also allows two receptors to contact a single HpHb dimer, allowing greater avidity for the ligand and more efficient uptake into trypanosomes (Lane-Serff et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Lane-Serff et al., 2014

claim: Specificity for HpHb results from direct, simultaneous contact between TbHpHbR and both haptoglobin and the β-subunit of haemoglobin.
source: Specificity for HpHb results from direct, simultaneous contact between the receptor and both haptoglobin and the β-subunit of haemoglobin.
evidence: Based on structural and binding data from previous studies

claim: Neither isolated haemoglobin nor haptoglobin binds significantly to TbHpHbR.
source: Neither isolated haemoglobin nor haptoglobin binds significantly (Vanhollebeke et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citation to Vanhollebeke et al., 2008

claim: The propionate chains of haem directly contact TbHpHbR and contribute to binding.
source: In addition, the propionate chains of haem directly contact the receptor and contribute to binding, with a significant reduction in binding affinity for HpHb that lacks haem (Stødkilde et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Stødkilde et al., 2014

claim: There is a significant reduction in binding affinity of TbHpHbR for HpHb that lacks haem.
source: In addition, the propionate chains of haem directly contact the receptor and contribute to binding, with a significant reduction in binding affinity for HpHb that lacks haem (Stødkilde et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Stødkilde et al., 2014

claim: TcHpHbR was identified by sequence homology to the receptor from T. brucei.
source: The T. congolense receptor (TcHpHbR) was identified by sequence homology to the receptor from T. brucei and also binds to HpHb with low micromolar affinity (a KD of 8 μM for TcHpHbR compared with 1 μM for TbHpHb) (Higgins et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Higgins et al., 2013

claim: TcHpHbR binds to HpHb with a KD of 8 μM.
source: The T. congolense receptor (TcHpHbR) was identified by sequence homology to the receptor from T. brucei and also binds to HpHb with low micromolar affinity (a KD of 8 μM for TcHpHbR compared with 1 μM for TbHpHb) (Higgins et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Higgins et al., 2013

claim: TbHpHbR binds to HpHb with a KD of 1 μM.
source: The T. congolense receptor (TcHpHbR) was identified by sequence homology to the receptor from T. brucei and also binds to HpHb with low micromolar affinity (a KD of 8 μM for TcHpHbR compared with 1 μM for TbHpHb) (Higgins et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Higgins et al., 2013

claim: TcHpHbR and TbHpHbR use overlapping binding sites to interact with HpHb.
source: Mutagenesis studies showed that TcHpHbR and TbHpHbR use overlapping binding sites to interact with HpHb (Higgins et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Higgins et al., 2013

claim: The structure of TcHpHbR has a similar architecture to TbHpHbR, with a long three α-helical bundle and small membrane-distal head.
source: The structure of TcHpHbR has a similar architecture to TbHpHbR, with a long three α-helical bundle and small membrane-distal head.
evidence: Based on structural data from previous studies

claim: The helical bundle of TcHpHbR lacks the kink found in TbHpHbR.
source: However, one striking difference is that the helical bundle of TcHpHbR lacks the kink found in TbHpHbR.
evidence: Based on structural data from previous studies

claim: Mixing TcHpHbR with HpSPHb results in disassembly of the HpSPHb complex and formation of a complex containing TcHpHbR and Hb.
source: However, analysis of the resulting fractions from the chromatography column revealed a higher molecular weight peak containing TcHpHbR and Hb, but no HpSP. A lower molecular weight peak, at the elution volume expected for unliganded TcHpHbR, contained excess free TcHpHbR and HpSP (Figure 1A).
evidence: Experimental data from gel filtration chromatography shown in Figure 1A

claim: TcHpHbR does not disassemble native HpHb complexes.
source: We therefore repeated the gel filtration experiment using native Hp in an HpHb complex. In this case, we found that the HpHb complex is not disassembled by incubation with the receptor, suggesting that the receptor does not disassemble native HpHb complexes during its physiological function (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Experimental data from gel filtration chromatography shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A

claim: TbHpHbR binds HpHb but not free Hb.
source: As expected, HpHbR from T. brucei interacted with HpHb, but not with Hb alone (Figure 1B).

claim: TcHpHbR interacts with either HpHb or free Hb.
source: However, HpHbRs from both T. congolense and T. vivax interacted with either HpHb or free Hb.
evidence: Experimental data from surface plasmon resonance

claim: TvHpHbR interacts with either HpHb or free Hb.
source: However, HpHbRs from both T. congolense and T. vivax interacted with either HpHb or free Hb.
evidence: Experimental data from surface plasmon resonance

claim: TcHpHbR and TvHpHbR form a far more stable complex with Hb than with HpHb, as shown by the lower off-rate.
source: Indeed, both receptors formed a far more stable complex with Hb than with HpHb, as shown by the lower off-rate (Figure 1B).
evidence: Experimental data from surface plasmon resonance shown in Figure 1B

claim: TcHpHbR forms a more stable complex with Hb than with HpHb.
source: In addition when Hb was mixed with TcHpHbR and subjected to gel filtration chromatography, the primary peak was a complex of TcHpHbR bound to Hb, indicating that TcHpHbR forms a more stable complex with Hb than with HpHb (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Experimental data from gel filtration chromatography shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B

claim: TcHpHbR binds to bovine haemoglobin with a strong interaction and slow off rate.
source: We therefore also tested the binding of TcHpHbR to bovine haemoglobin and observed a strong interaction with a slow off rate (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).

claim: Two TcHpHbR molecules interact with one Hb tetramer.
source: This revealed that two receptors interact with one Hb tetramer.

claim: The KD for the TcHpHbR:Hb interaction is 3 nM.
source: The KD for the TcHpHbR:Hb interaction was estimated to be 3 nM by ITC.

claim: The affinity of TcHpHbR for Hb is around 1000-fold tighter than its affinity for HpHb.
source: This is around 1000-fold tighter than the affinity of the same receptor for HpHb, previously measured by ITC to be 3 μM (Higgins et al., 2013).

claim: T. congolense and T. brucei diverged from each other after their last common ancestor had diverged from T. vivax.
source: T. congolense and T. brucei diverged from each other after their last common ancestor had diverged from T. vivax (Figure 1D) (Stevens et al., 1999; Hamilton et al., 2004; Kelly et al., 2014).

claim: Hb binding was lost from T. brucei after it diverged from T. congolense rather than separately gained in both T. congolense and T. vivax.
source: As HpHbRs from both T. congolense and T. vivax bind to Hb, it is most likely that this property was lost from T. brucei after it diverged from T. congolense rather than separately gained in both T. congolense and T. vivax.

claim: The ancestor of the HpHbRs was primarily a haemoglobin receptor.
source: Together these observations suggest that the ancestor of the HpHbRs was primarily a haemoglobin receptor and that evolutionary changes that have taken place during the evolution of T. brucei have led to an alteration in its binding specificity.

claim: Evolutionary changes during the evolution of T. brucei have led to an alteration in HpHbR binding specificity.
source: Together these observations suggest that the ancestor of the HpHbRs was primarily a haemoglobin receptor and that evolutionary changes that have taken place during the evolution of T. brucei have led to an alteration in its binding specificity.

claim: A previous proteomic analysis did not detect TcHpHbR protein in bloodstream forms but did detect it as an abundant protein in epimastigotes.

claim: A transcriptome analysis of T. vivax indicated that TvHpHbR mRNA was most abundant in epimastigotes.
source: In addition, a transcriptome analysis of various developmental forms of T. vivax indicated that TvHpHbR mRNA was most abundant in epimastigotes (Jackson et al., 2015).

claim: Western blot analysis showed expression of TcHpHbR in three independently generated epimastigote-containing cultures.

claim: TcHpHbR expression was below detectable levels in procyclic cells or in bloodstream form T. congolense.
source: Western blot analysis of three independently generated epimastigote-containing cultures showed expression of the TcHpHbR in these populations, while expression was below detectable levels in the original procyclic cells or in bloodstream form T. congolense (Figure 2; Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Experimental data from western blot shown in Figure 2 and Figure 2—figure supplement 1

claim: Differentiation to the epimastigote form was associated with expression of TcHpHbR.
source: Therefore differentiation to the epimastigote form was associated with expression of TcHpHbR.

claim: In all cells in which kinetoplast repositioning to that found in the epimastigote form had occurred, TcHpHbR protein was detected and localised across the whole cell surface, including the flagellum.
source: In all cells in which kinetoplast repositioning to that found in the epimastigote form had occurred, TcHpHbR protein was detected and localised across the whole cell surface, including the flagellum, in both permeabilised and non-permeabilised cells (Figure 3A and B).

claim: Trypanosomes harvested from the midgut were all negative for TcHpHbR staining.

claim: Trypomastigotes from the proventriculus were typically negative for TcHpHbR staining.

claim: All epimastigotes from the tsetse proboscis had high levels of TcHpHbR expression.
source: All epimastigotes identified had high levels of TcHpHbR expression, whereas trypomastigotes were either negative or weakly positive (Figure 3C, lower three panels).

claim: TcHpHbR is highly expressed in the T. congolense epimastigote life-stage in vivo.
source: Therefore, TcHpHbR is highly expressed in the T. congolense epimastigote life-stage in vivo, with some upregulation of expression occurring prior to kinetoplast repositioning.

claim: The average copy number of TcHpHbR is approximately 5–9 x 10^5 molecules per TcHpHbR-expressing cell.

claim: T. brucei bloodstream forms express approximately 200 to 400 TbHpHbR molecules per cell.

claim: T. congolense HpHbR has around a 1000-fold more receptors per cell than are found in the T. brucei bloodstream form.

claim: The T. congolense developmental form that highly expresses the TcHpHbR on its surface is able to internalise Hb at low nanomolar concentrations.

claim: A complete data set for the TcHpHbR:Hb complex was collected to 3.2 Å resolution.
source: This complex crystallised with a well solution of 8% PEG 8000, 0.1 M sodium citrate pH 5.0 in 18 hr, and a complete data set was collected to 3.2 Å resolution.

claim: Each TcHpHbR receptor makes the same interactions with haemoglobin.

claim: The receptor conformation of TcHpHbR is unaltered from that of unliganded receptor, with a root-mean-square deviation of 0.6 Å.

claim: The haemoglobin in the TcHpHbR:Hb complex is in the oxygenated conformation with a root-mean-square deviation of 0.7 Å from the search model.

claim: The interaction surface between TcHpHbR and Hb can be divided into two subsites, with interactions made with the α-subunit of one haemoglobin dimer and the β-subunit of the second haemoglobin dimer.

claim: TcHpHbR either binds selectively to haemoglobin tetramers or two haemoglobin dimers will assemble together with the receptor.

claim: The haemoglobin molecules of most of the mammals bitten by tsetse flies will bind to TcHpHbR.

claim: The membrane-proximal binding site of TcHpHbR contacts the β-subunit of haemoglobin with a total contact surface area of 650 Å2.

claim: The propionate chains of haem directly interact with the receptor at the membrane-proximal binding site.
